title: Polyanion-stabilized amorphous halide electrolytes with low lithium content for all-solid-state lithium batteries

paper_content.abstract:
Lithium halide solid electrolytes have garnered significant attention owing to their high ionic
conductivity and positive electrode compatibility. However, achieving target ionic conductivity
typically requires high lithium concentration (> 4.3 wt%) within optimal structure, which raises
costs and exacerbates air sensitivity. Here, we leverage anion clusters to synthesize a series of
amorphous halide electrolytes xLi SO -ZrCl , with optimal ionic conductivities of 1.5 mS cm-1 at
2 4 4
30 ℃ and a significantly reduced lithium content of 2.4 wt%, alongside good air stability. Through
neutron/synchrotron X-ray experiments, first-principles calculations and machine learning-
accelerated molecular dynamics simulations, we reveal a disordered backbone of [Zr Cl (SO )]2-
a 4a 4
(1 ≤ a ≤ 4) that enables fast Li-ion diffusion via under-coordinated oxygen sites. All-solid-state
lithium batteries employing these electrolytes and LiNi Co Mn O positive electrode exhibit
0.8 0.1 0.1 2
81.1% capacity retention after 1400 cycles at 1 C (60 min) and 30 ℃. Our findings reveal anion-
cluster chemistry as an approach that transforms solid electrolyte design for advanced batteries,
bridging materials science with practical energy storage innovation.
paper_content.introduction:
Next-generation electronics and electric vehicles demand advanced all-solid-state lithium
batteries (ASSLBs) for their safety, high energy density, and long cycle life1, 2. The cornerstone of
ASSLB technology is the development of Li-ion solid electrolytes (SEs).3 Oxides, sulfides and
halides, have been explored over the past decades4, 5. Oxides (e.g., Li La Zr O ) exhibit excellent
7 3 2 12
thermal and oxidative stability, but require high-temperature sintering due to their rigidity
structure6-8. Sulfides (e.g., Li GeP S , Li PS Cl ), while offering high room-temperature
10 2 12 6-x 5-x 1+x
ionic conductivity via cold pressing, have limited electrochemical stability and poor environmental
resistance9-11. Halide SEs, commonly represented by ternary Li-M-X systems (M = Y, In, Sc, Zr,
Sm, La, Al, Ta, or Nb; X = F, Cl, Br, or I), have garnered significant research interest due to their
high ionic conductivity, wide electrochemical window, and reasonable deformability12, 13,14-27.
Lithium concentration is a key factor influencing ionic conduction in Li-M-X SEs. In general,
a high lithium content (> 4.3 wt%) is required in these high-conducting halide SEs, as shown in
Fig. 1c. For instance, Li ZrCl 28is a promising low-cost SE but has a limited ionic conductivity of
2 6
~0.4 mS cm-1. Substitution of ZrI4+ by trivalent cations (e.g., Fe3+, In3+, Sc3+, or Al3+)28-30 increases
lithium content, enhancing ionic conductivity from 0.4 mS cm-1 to typically > 1.0 mS cm-1.
Theoretical study suggests that an optimal 40-60% Li octahedral occupancy (corresponding to a
lithium weight percentage of ~4.8-6.7% in representative halides, Supplementary Table 1) is
crucial for achieving high ionic conduction in close-packed halide SEs 31. Very recently, this
finding has been verified experimentally32. However, achieving high conductivity while reducing
lithium content remains a significant challenge.

The high lithium content will increase the SE cost, especially when considering the limited
global lithium reserves (Supplementary Fig. 1) and their upward fluctuations33. For example, the
price of LiCl (anhydrous, 98%) in 2024 (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3) is about 20 times higher
than that in 202134. Therefore, it is crucial to explore new strategies for decreasing a SE's ultimate
cost by decreasing lithium content, owing to the multiple variables like supply-demand
fluctuations, synthesis and manufacturing complexities, etc5. Additionally, reducing the Li-ion
content is crucial for improving the air stability of SE, as the high charge density of small Li+
cations leads to strong electrostatic interactions with polar H O molecules35. As a result,
2
spontaneous hydrolysis reactions occur when halide SEs are exposed to air, leading to a drastic
decay in performance, as seen in all reported halide SEs36-38. This issue presents a significant
challenge for large-scale production and processing.

In this work, we report a family of low-lithium-content amorphous SEs by combining clusters
of [SO ]2- and [ZrCl ] using a simple ball milling method. By regulating the anion proportions,
4 4
these materials achieve a significantly reduced Li content of 2.4 wt% while maintaining high Li+
conductivity of 1.5 mS cm-1 at 30 ℃. To uncover the structural origin of the high conductivity in
this low-lithium-content amorphous system, we performed pair distribution function (PDF)
analysis based on the neutron total scattering and synchrotron X-ray data, integrated with multi-
scale modeling under a self-constructed accurate and efficient workflow, including first-principles
calculations and molecular dynamics simulations (MD) based on machine-learning force field
(MLFF). We revealed an interesting, disordered backbone consisting of four complex anions
clusters of [Zr Cl (SO )]2- (1 ≤ a ≤ 4) interconnected by sulfate ions, forming a percolation
a 4a 4
network for Li-ion with frustrated energy landscapes. The ionic conduction in the amorphous
electrolyte is primarily attributed to Li-ion hopping between sites with low oxygen coordination.
ASSLBs utilizing the SEs and LiNi Co Mn O positive electrode demonstrate good cycling
0.8 0.1 0.1 2
stability for over 1400 cycles at 1.0 C and 30 ℃. In addition, the SEs deliver decent air stability
under 30% relative humidity. Our work redefines the design paradigm for halide SEs,
demonstrating that strategic anion-cluster manipulation in amorphous systems can circumvent
traditional lithium-content limitations, thereby advancing cost-effective, high-energy-density all-
solid-state batteries.

Li+transport mechanism
The Arrhenius relation for the amorphous structure was calculated based on the MLFF-MD
(see Methods). As shown in Fig. 3g, by analyzing the region where the mean squared displacement
(MSD) curves exhibit a linear time dependence (Supplementary Fig. 24–25), the room-temperature
ionic conductivity based on a 3-ns MLFF-MD simulation is about 1.7 mS cm-1, close to the
experimental value of 1.5 mS cm-1. The activation energy derived from the simulation is 0.32 eV,
which is in good agreement with experimental results (0.33 eV), further confirming the reliability
of our computational results.

To elucidate the conduction mechanism of Li+ in the disordered framework, we initially
examined the coordination environment of Li+. As shown in Fig. 3f, the coordination environment
is complex and can be classified into four main types based on the number of coordinating oxygen
atoms: (i) oxygen-free sites labeled as Li-Cl (x = 1-5), (ii) single-oxygen-coordinated Li-Cl O (x
x x
= 1-4), (iii) double-oxygen-coordinated Li-Cl O (x = 1-4), and (iv) triple-oxygen-coordinated Li-
x 2
Cl O (x = 0-2). These coordination environments evolve over time due to the mobility of Li+ that
x 3
is dictated by the kinetic energy of Li+ and the potential energy surface, potentially giving rise to
more than a dozen distinct coordination environments, including Li-Cl , Li-Cl , Li-Cl O, and Li-
5 4 3
Cl O, among others. All these local Li+ environments lack the periodically arranged LiCl
2 6
sublattice observed in Li ZrCl , instead adopting a fully disordered configuration. Notably, the
2 6
presence of diverse Li⁺ coordination environments creates a frustrated energy landscape50, which
promotes fast ionic conduction by facilitating percolation networks for Li⁺ transport. The spatial
distribution of Li+ probability at 300 K over the 3-ns trajectory in Fig. 3h reveals a percolating
isotropic diffusion pattern, indicating efficient Li⁺ transport through interconnected pathways.
Furthermore, in this amorphous framework, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 26a-b, approximately
50% of Li+ exhibit diffusion distances exceeding 2 Å, alongside 5% achieving distances greater
than 8 Å in this frustrated energy landscape over the 3-ns trajectory. These diffusion processes are
correlated with oxygen coordination. The shorter Li–O bond length (~2.0 Å compared to ~2.5 Å
of Li–Cl from radial distribution functions in Supplementary Fig. 26e) arises from stronger Li–O
interactions, which suggests that lower oxygen coordination environments favor Li+ diffusion, a
trend corroborated by statistical analysis in Supplementary Fig. 26c. In summary, the amorphous
framework creates various Li+ coordination environments that homogenizes the energy landscape,
thereby enabling room-temperature superionic conductivity.

Cell performance
In addition to the high ionic conductivity, the 0.5Li SO -ZrCl SE also possess favorable
2 4 4
deformability and good oxidation stability, which are two critical attributes for achieving high-
energy density ASSLBs. The powder and pellet morphologies of 0.5Li SO -ZrCl were examined
2 4 4
by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). As displayed in Supplementary Fig. 27, the powder
samples, hundreds of nanometers to a few micrometers in size, can be easily cold-pressed into
dense pellets, indicating good deformability. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) was further
employed to assess the Young’s modulus of 0.5Li SO -ZrCl , revealing a low average Young’s
2 4 4
modulus of ~2.0 GPa (Supplementary Fig. 28), a value comparable to the representative soft
electrolytes of AlOCl-LiCl51 and Li-Ta-Cl52, and lower than that of sulfide SEs (20 GPa)53. This
low Young’s modulus ensures tight contact between SE particles, which is essential for minimizing
interfacial resistance in ASSLBs. Moreover, the electrochemical stability of 0.5Li SO -ZrCl SE
2 4 4
was evaluated through linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 29. The
oxidation stability of 0.5Li SO -ZrCl is ~4.4 V vs. Li/Li+, which is identical to the calculated
2 4 4
value (Supplementary Figs. 30-31), and higher than that of sulfide SEs (~2.4 V vs. Li/Li+) and
competitive compared to the reported halides (~4.3 V vs. Li/Li+)14, 54.

1.0 C, respectively. Additionally, the specific discharge capacity of the full cell can recover to

mg cm-2. These achieved a high initial areal capacity of 6.4 mAh cm-2, and a robust capacity
retention of 82.4% after 300 cycles (5.3 mAh cm-2). Moreover, full cell with the 0.5Li SO -ZrCl
2 4 4
SE also can even endure a higher charge cut-off voltage of 4.6 V (Fig. 4f), delivering an initial

100 cycles. The SE also enabled stable cycle performance with LiCoO positive electrode
2
(Supplementary Figs. 32-35 and Supplementary Table 11). Overall, the performance of 0.5Li SO -
2 4
ZrCl -based cells is competitive with other representative halide SEs (Supplementary Table 10),
4
underscoring its potential for high-energy-density ASSLBs.

2 4 4
combines a low lithium content of 2.4 wt% with good performance. The 0.5Li SO -ZrCl SE
2 4 4
exhibits a high ionic conductivity of 1.5 mS cm-1, at 30 ℃. This conductivity can be ascribed to

amorphous atomic structure without empirical parameters. The calculated pair distribution
function and temperature-dependent ionic conductivity show good agreement with experimental

[Zr Cl (SO )]2- framework, where a reduced oxygen coordination is associated with enhanced
a 4a 4

ZrCl at 30% RH. This anion-clustering strategy addresses key challenges of cost and stability for
4

SEs with the general formula xLi SO -ZrCl (0 < x ≤ 1.0) were synthesized via a mechanochemical
2 4 4

2 4 4
99.5%) were used as the raw materials. For comparative studies, LiCl (Aladdin, 99.5%) replaced
Li SO to prepare 2xLiCl-ZrCl . The starting materials were mixed in an argon-filled glovebox
2 4 4
(H O < 0.01ppm, O < 0.01ppm). Then, each mixture (1 g) was processed in a zirconia jar with 30
2 2
g grinding media using a FRITSCH Pulverisette 7 planetary mill. The milling protocol consisted
of 500 rpm operation for 15 min, followed by 5 min pauses, with this cycle repeated for a total of
50 times. After ball-milling, the products were transferred into the glovebox for further use.

The raw material costs for large-scale production (1000 kg) were estimated using the quantity-
price scaling model55. This model relates the unit price (P) and purchase (Q) quantity through:

1.5406 Å). Samples were sealed in Kapton films to prevent air/moisture exposure during
measurement. The neutron total scattering data were acquired on the multi-physics instrument
using a high-intensity time-of-flight diffractometer at the China Neutron Spallation Source (CSNS).
The high-energy X-ray total scattering test was conducted at BL08, SPring-8 in Japan, utilizing a
16-inch two-dimensional detector (XRD1621) with a wavelength of 0.1087 Å. The simulated
nPDF and sPDF G(r) values from CIF files are calculated by PDF gui software56. Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) images were acquired using a Hitachi S-4800 field emission SEM equipped
with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). Microstructures were further observed via
transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Talos F200X G2). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
(XPS) data were recorded using a Thermo Scientific K-Alpha Spectrometer with a monochromatic
Al Kα source. Raman spectra were obtained using a HORIBA Scientific LabRAM HR Raman
spectrometer system (532.4 nm laser). X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements were
performed at BL11B of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). An atomic force

which were formed under a pressure of 2 tons. For force spectroscopy measurements, an AFM tip
(Bruker Corp.) with a spring constant (k) of 200 N·m-1 and a resonance frequency (f ) of 525 kHz
0
was utilized.

Conductivity measurements
Prior to conductivity measurements, ~100 mg of the SE powders was placed in a
polyetheretherketone (PEEK) mold (diameter 10 mm), and cold-pressed to form pellets under a
pressure of 3 tons for 1 min using a hydraulic press (Xinnuo Instruments, SYP-12B). The thickness
of the resulting pellets was controlled within the range of 0.06-0.07 cm. All pellet preparation steps
were conducted in an argon-filled glovebox with water and oxygen contents < 0.01 ppm. Ionic
conductivity of the SE pellets was evaluated via EIS using a symmetric cell configuration with
two stainless steel rods as blocking electrodes. EIS measurements were performed on a Bio-Logic
MTZ-35 analyzer over a frequency range of 7 MHz to 1Hz with alternating current (AC) amplitude
of 10 mV. A total of 10 data points were collected per frequency decade to ensure sufficient data
resolution. Electronic conductivity was assessed through a direct current (DC) polarization
measurement. In this measurement, a voltage of 1.0 V was applied to the same symmetric cells.
All these measurements temperature control was realized in an environment test chamber.

Computational details
Reactions between anion clusters. The AIMD unit reactions of ZrCl and Li SO were calculated
4 2 4
in ORCA57-59 using the r2SCAN-3c60 composite electronic-structure method (r2SCAN functional61
with triple-ζ Gaussian atomic orbital basis set plus refitted Grimme’s D4 dispersion62 and
geometrical counter-poise corrections (gCP)63 for London-dispersion and basis set superposition
error). Def2/J acceleration64 is enabled for the formation of the Coulomb matrix in the calculation.
To investigate the dynamic behavior of these reactions, AIMD simulations were conducted in the
NVT (constant particle number N, constant volume V and a temperature fluctuating around an
equilibrium value T) ensemble at 350 K with a time step of 1.5 fs for 3000 steps, resulting in the
generation of two structural cluster units.

Construction of training dataset: The training dataset was constructed via fourth-iterative
(detailed in Supplementary Fig. 20) sampling AIMD trajectories from supercells containing 8
cluster units ([Li Zr Cl SO ] ) using the CP2K software65. Simulations employed the r2SCAN
2 2 8 4 8
functional61 with optimized norm-conserving Goedecker-Teter-Hutter pseudopotentials66 and the
matched double-zeta polarized basis set67 within the framework of Gaussian Plane Waves (GPW).
A plane-wave cutoff of 500 Ry was applied and each Gaussian function was mapped onto a grid
with a cutoff of 60 Ry. Orbital transformation (OT) method68 was used to facilitate convergence.
The self-consistent field energy was converged to a criterion of 1×10-5 Hartree. NVT AIMD
simulations were performed from 300 K to 1200 K using the Bussi-Donadio-Parrinello (BDP)
thermostat with a time step of 3 fs. All AIMD trajectory snapshots were recorded every two steps.

Machine learning force-filed finetuning. MLFF was constructed in the MACE framework69. We
employed MACE-matpes-r2scan-omat-ft as base model and subsequently fine-tuned it for our
specific system (detailed in Supplementary Fig. 20). The training dataset were randomly
partitioned into 75% training, 5% validating and 20% testing sets. During fine-tuning, all model
parameters remained frozen, with loss weights set to 1 for energy, 10 for forces, and 100 for stress.
As shown in Supplementary Fig. 21, the root mean square error (RMSE) of the MLFF model for
energy, forces and stresses is 0.4 meV/atom, 20.8 meV/Å and 254.5 bar, respectively, with R-
squared values of 0.9838, 0.9990, and 0.9929.

2 2 8 4 64

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
We thank the authors for their detailed response to our review. After reading the revised manuscript, our original concerns
have been sufficiently addressed. The updated version provides clearer justification of the novelty and offers stronger
support for their discussions and conclusions. We appreciate the additional effort taken to update figures, explain
methodology choices, and strengthen the experimental validation. Overall, we believe the manuscript has been significantly
improved and we recommend its publication in Nature Communication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature
Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career
Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors have addressed my concerns. I have no further comments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The author provided lots of extra information in the revised manuscript, which is greatly appreciated. However, some
comments are not addressed well, and a few puzzles need to be addressed further.
1. The response to comment 4 of reviewer 3 is not relevant. The comment is “Please clarify the designing principle involving
SO42- instead of other polyanions.”, but the authors’ response is not relevant to other polyanions at all.
2. The high energy of mechanochemical ball milling could plausibly induce the decomposition of the sulfate group, leading to
the evolution of SO2 gas and the formation of an oxychloride rather than the proposed polyanion-stabilized structure.
Therefore, it is highly necessary to perform gas mass spectrometry analysis of the atmosphere inside the milling jar after ball
milling. In addition, it is strongly recommended that the authors conduct a quantitative elemental analysis on the final product
to confirm that the molar ratio of Sulfur (S) to Zirconium (Zr) aligns with the stoichiometric input, which would directly refute
the possibility of sulfur loss and provide more robust support for the manuscript's central claim.
3. The authors used LiCl–ZrCl4 as a reference for comparison with Li2SO4-ZrCl4. It should be noted that Li2SO4-ZrCl4
exhibited an amorphous structure, whereas LiCl-ZrCl4 remained crystalline. Directly comparing their ionic conductivities is
therefore not entirely fair. According to most of the relevant literature, amorphous halide solid electrolytes typically exhibit
much higher ionic conductivities than their crystalline counterparts (e.g., amorphous LiTaCl6: 10.95 mS/cm (Chem. Lett. 2023,
52, 237–241) vs. crystallized LiTaCl6: ≈10 -5 mS/cm (Adv. Energy Mater. 2024, 14, 2402555); crystallized NaTaCl6:
≈10 -3 mS/cm vs. amorphous NaTaCl6: ≈4 mS/cm (Matter 2024, 7, 1018–1034); crystallized NaNbCl4O: 0.1 mS/cm (Angew.
Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, e202416979) vs. amorphous NaNbCl4O: ≈1 mS/cm (Small 2025, 21, 2504677)). Therefore, it is
recommended to extend the ball-milling duration to synthesize amorphous LiCl-ZrCl4 and then perform a direct comparison
with Li₂SO4-ZrCl4 under similar structural states.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
The authors have provided extensive experimental data and analyses in response to the reviewers’ comments. While the
responses are extensive, the explanations related to moisture stability and the Li+ transport mechanism still leave certain
points insufficiently addressed.
1. The authors experimentally demonstrate that 0.5Li₂SO₄-ZrCl₄ exhibits enhanced moisture stability through in situ XRD
and DEMS. However, the computational results do not appear to sufficiently support this conclusion. (1) How the initial
structures were defined for calculating the reaction energies of 2LiCl-ZrCl4 and 0.5Li2SO4-ZrCl4 is not clearly explained
and requires clarification. This is because the calculated DFT energies show large deviations depending on the structural
configuration. It is also necessary to clarify whether the energies of various compounds were calculated using structures
taken from the MP Database. (2) Moreover, the reported positive hydrolysis reaction energies would generally indicate that
reactions with H2O are unfavorable (ΔG > 0). An energetically non-spontaneous state implies that decomposition does not
occur in either case. (3) In addition, since the differences in calculated ΔG values for ZrOCl2 and ZrO2 formation between
0.5Li2SO4-ZrCl4 and 2LiCl-ZrCl4 are only ~0.03 eV, it is unclear whether such a small variation can be regarded as
significant within the accuracy limits of DFT calculations.
2. The authors suggest that Li⁺ ions with fewer initial oxygen coordinations are more likely to undergo long-range diffusion in
0.5Li₂SO₄–ZrCl₄, and they suggest that the beneficial effect of amorphization outweighs the negative impact of oxygen.
However, considering that the Li/O ratio scales directly with composition in xLi2SO4–ZrCl4, it remains unclear how a
reduced Li concentration in a low-Li compound such as 0.5LiSO4–ZrCl4 could still promote ionic conduction despite the
trapping effect of oxygen and fewer carrier concentration. The explanation for why 0.5LiSO4–ZrCl4, in the presence of
oxygen potential wells, nonetheless exhibits enhanced Li⁺ transport therefore remains unconvincing. To rigorously verify the
role of oxygen, a direct comparative model (e.g., 0.5LiSO4–ZrCl4 vs. LiSO4–ZrCl4) should be considered. Furthermore, if
oxygen incorporation is intrinsically detrimental to conduction, one might expect that in oxygen-free systems such as 1LiCl–
ZrCl4, extended ball-milling could induce amorphization that achieves superior transport properties, highlighting the need for
a more systematic comparison with compositions like xLiCl–ZrCl with xLiSO4–ZrCl4 to substantiate the authors’ claim.
3. It is impressive that the authors were able to investigate the detailed mechanisms of amorphous structures at a broader
scale using MLFF, which would be inaccessible by AIMD. However, the explanation of these mechanisms fundamentally
rests on the assumption that the MLFF model achieves very high accuracy. In this regard, the present work only discloses
validation-set results for MLFF, and the study would become more complete if additional verifications of the MLFF were
provided. Specifically, in Supplementary Fig. 21 the accuracy of MLFF is evaluated using the validation set. Yet, since the
validation set is already used during training for loss comparison, it is important to also report how well the model performs
on an independent test set. According to Liu et al. (npj Comput. Mater. 9, 174 (2023)), even if the MAE or RMSE of forces
appear small, these averaged metrics often fail to capture the occasional large errors in specific trajectories during MD
simulations. Therefore, a more detailed comparison of errors in both the magnitude and direction of forces would be
valuable. Furthermore, it would be helpful to include additional validations such as the force softening scale recently
proposed (Deng et al., npj Comput. Mater. 11, 9 (2025)), or out-of-distribution and phonon DOS tests as in recent MLFF
studies (Ding et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 118–125 (2025)). Incorporating such validations would significantly strengthen
confidence in the MLFF model and, consequently, the proposed mechanistic insights.

## Introduction

Next-generation electronics and electric vehicles demand advanced all-solid-state lithium
batteries (ASSLBs) for their safety, high energy density, and long cycle life1, 2. The cornerstone of
ASSLB technology is the development of Li-ion solid electrolytes (SEs).3 Oxides, sulfides and
halides, have been explored over the past decades4, 5. Oxides (e.g., Li La Zr O ) exhibit excellent
7 3 2 12
thermal and oxidative stability, but require high-temperature sintering due to their rigidity
structure6-8. Sulfides (e.g., Li GeP S , Li PS Cl ), while offering high room-temperature
10 2 12 6-x 5-x 1+x
ionic conductivity via cold pressing, have limited electrochemical stability and poor environmental
resistance9-11. Halide SEs, commonly represented by ternary Li-M-X systems (M = Y, In, Sc, Zr,
Sm, La, Al, Ta, or Nb; X = F, Cl, Br, or I), have garnered significant research interest due to their
high ionic conductivity, wide electrochemical window, and reasonable deformability12, 13,14-27.
Lithium concentration is a key factor influencing ionic conduction in Li-M-X SEs. In general,
a high lithium content (> 4.3 wt%) is required in these high-conducting halide SEs, as shown in
Fig. 1c. For instance, Li ZrCl 28is a promising low-cost SE but has a limited ionic conductivity of
2 6
~0.4 mS cm-1. Substitution of ZrI4+ by trivalent cations (e.g., Fe3+, In3+, Sc3+, or Al3+)28-30 increases
lithium content, enhancing ionic conductivity from 0.4 mS cm-1 to typically > 1.0 mS cm-1.
Theoretical study suggests that an optimal 40-60% Li octahedral occupancy (corresponding to a
lithium weight percentage of ~4.8-6.7% in representative halides, Supplementary Table 1) is
crucial for achieving high ionic conduction in close-packed halide SEs 31. Very recently, this
finding has been verified experimentally32. However, achieving high conductivity while reducing
lithium content remains a significant challenge.

The high lithium content will increase the SE cost, especially when considering the limited
global lithium reserves (Supplementary Fig. 1) and their upward fluctuations33. For example, the
price of LiCl (anhydrous, 98%) in 2024 (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3) is about 20 times higher
than that in 202134. Therefore, it is crucial to explore new strategies for decreasing a SE's ultimate
cost by decreasing lithium content, owing to the multiple variables like supply-demand
fluctuations, synthesis and manufacturing complexities, etc5. Additionally, reducing the Li-ion
content is crucial for improving the air stability of SE, as the high charge density of small Li+
cations leads to strong electrostatic interactions with polar H O molecules35. As a result,
2
spontaneous hydrolysis reactions occur when halide SEs are exposed to air, leading to a drastic
decay in performance, as seen in all reported halide SEs36-38. This issue presents a significant
challenge for large-scale production and processing.

In this work, we report a family of low-lithium-content amorphous SEs by combining clusters
of [SO ]2- and [ZrCl ] using a simple ball milling method. By regulating the anion proportions,
4 4
these materials achieve a significantly reduced Li content of 2.4 wt% while maintaining high Li+
conductivity of 1.5 mS cm-1 at 30 ℃. To uncover the structural origin of the high conductivity in
this low-lithium-content amorphous system, we performed pair distribution function (PDF)
analysis based on the neutron total scattering and synchrotron X-ray data, integrated with multi-
scale modeling under a self-constructed accurate and efficient workflow, including first-principles
calculations and molecular dynamics simulations (MD) based on machine-learning force field
(MLFF). We revealed an interesting, disordered backbone consisting of four complex anions
clusters of [Zr Cl (SO )]2- (1 ≤ a ≤ 4) interconnected by sulfate ions, forming a percolation
a 4a 4
network for Li-ion with frustrated energy landscapes. The ionic conduction in the amorphous
electrolyte is primarily attributed to Li-ion hopping between sites with low oxygen coordination.
ASSLBs utilizing the SEs and LiNi Co Mn O positive electrode demonstrate good cycling
0.8 0.1 0.1 2
stability for over 1400 cycles at 1.0 C and 30 ℃. In addition, the SEs deliver decent air stability
under 30% relative humidity. Our work redefines the design paradigm for halide SEs,
demonstrating that strategic anion-cluster manipulation in amorphous systems can circumvent
traditional lithium-content limitations, thereby advancing cost-effective, high-energy-density all-
solid-state batteries.

### Reviewer 1

We thank the authors for their detailed response to our review. After reading the revised manuscript, our original concerns
have been sufficiently addressed. The updated version provides clearer justification of the novelty and offers stronger
support for their discussions and conclusions. We appreciate the additional effort taken to update figures, explain
methodology choices, and strengthen the experimental validation. Overall, we believe the manuscript has been significantly
improved and we recommend its publication in Nature Communication.

### Reviewer 2

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature
Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career
Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have addressed my concerns. I have no further comments.

### Reviewer 4

The author provided lots of extra information in the revised manuscript, which is greatly appreciated. However, some
comments are not addressed well, and a few puzzles need to be addressed further.
1. The response to comment 4 of reviewer 3 is not relevant. The comment is “Please clarify the designing principle involving
SO42- instead of other polyanions.”, but the authors’ response is not relevant to other polyanions at all.
2. The high energy of mechanochemical ball milling could plausibly induce the decomposition of the sulfate group, leading to
the evolution of SO2 gas and the formation of an oxychloride rather than the proposed polyanion-stabilized structure.
Therefore, it is highly necessary to perform gas mass spectrometry analysis of the atmosphere inside the milling jar after ball
milling. In addition, it is strongly recommended that the authors conduct a quantitative elemental analysis on the final product
to confirm that the molar ratio of Sulfur (S) to Zirconium (Zr) aligns with the stoichiometric input, which would directly refute
the possibility of sulfur loss and provide more robust support for the manuscript's central claim.
3. The authors used LiCl–ZrCl4 as a reference for comparison with Li2SO4-ZrCl4. It should be noted that Li2SO4-ZrCl4
exhibited an amorphous structure, whereas LiCl-ZrCl4 remained crystalline. Directly comparing their ionic conductivities is
therefore not entirely fair. According to most of the relevant literature, amorphous halide solid electrolytes typically exhibit
much higher ionic conductivities than their crystalline counterparts (e.g., amorphous LiTaCl6: 10.95 mS/cm (Chem. Lett. 2023,
52, 237–241) vs. crystallized LiTaCl6: ≈10 -5 mS/cm (Adv. Energy Mater. 2024, 14, 2402555); crystallized NaTaCl6:
≈10 -3 mS/cm vs. amorphous NaTaCl6: ≈4 mS/cm (Matter 2024, 7, 1018–1034); crystallized NaNbCl4O: 0.1 mS/cm (Angew.
Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, e202416979) vs. amorphous NaNbCl4O: ≈1 mS/cm (Small 2025, 21, 2504677)). Therefore, it is
recommended to extend the ball-milling duration to synthesize amorphous LiCl-ZrCl4 and then perform a direct comparison
with Li₂SO4-ZrCl4 under similar structural states.

### Reviewer 5

The authors have provided extensive experimental data and analyses in response to the reviewers’ comments. While the
responses are extensive, the explanations related to moisture stability and the Li+ transport mechanism still leave certain
points insufficiently addressed.
1. The authors experimentally demonstrate that 0.5Li₂SO₄-ZrCl₄ exhibits enhanced moisture stability through in situ XRD
and DEMS. However, the computational results do not appear to sufficiently support this conclusion. (1) How the initial
structures were defined for calculating the reaction energies of 2LiCl-ZrCl4 and 0.5Li2SO4-ZrCl4 is not clearly explained
and requires clarification. This is because the calculated DFT energies show large deviations depending on the structural
configuration. It is also necessary to clarify whether the energies of various compounds were calculated using structures
taken from the MP Database. (2) Moreover, the reported positive hydrolysis reaction energies would generally indicate that
reactions with H2O are unfavorable (ΔG > 0). An energetically non-spontaneous state implies that decomposition does not
occur in either case. (3) In addition, since the differences in calculated ΔG values for ZrOCl2 and ZrO2 formation between
0.5Li2SO4-ZrCl4 and 2LiCl-ZrCl4 are only ~0.03 eV, it is unclear whether such a small variation can be regarded as
significant within the accuracy limits of DFT calculations.
2. The authors suggest that Li⁺ ions with fewer initial oxygen coordinations are more likely to undergo long-range diffusion in
0.5Li₂SO₄–ZrCl₄, and they suggest that the beneficial effect of amorphization outweighs the negative impact of oxygen.
However, considering that the Li/O ratio scales directly with composition in xLi2SO4–ZrCl4, it remains unclear how a
reduced Li concentration in a low-Li compound such as 0.5LiSO4–ZrCl4 could still promote ionic conduction despite the
trapping effect of oxygen and fewer carrier concentration. The explanation for why 0.5LiSO4–ZrCl4, in the presence of
oxygen potential wells, nonetheless exhibits enhanced Li⁺ transport therefore remains unconvincing. To rigorously verify the
role of oxygen, a direct comparative model (e.g., 0.5LiSO4–ZrCl4 vs. LiSO4–ZrCl4) should be considered. Furthermore, if
oxygen incorporation is intrinsically detrimental to conduction, one might expect that in oxygen-free systems such as 1LiCl–
ZrCl4, extended ball-milling could induce amorphization that achieves superior transport properties, highlighting the need for
a more systematic comparison with compositions like xLiCl–ZrCl with xLiSO4–ZrCl4 to substantiate the authors’ claim.
3. It is impressive that the authors were able to investigate the detailed mechanisms of amorphous structures at a broader
scale using MLFF, which would be inaccessible by AIMD. However, the explanation of these mechanisms fundamentally
rests on the assumption that the MLFF model achieves very high accuracy. In this regard, the present work only discloses
validation-set results for MLFF, and the study would become more complete if additional verifications of the MLFF were
provided. Specifically, in Supplementary Fig. 21 the accuracy of MLFF is evaluated using the validation set. Yet, since the
validation set is already used during training for loss comparison, it is important to also report how well the model performs
on an independent test set. According to Liu et al. (npj Comput. Mater. 9, 174 (2023)), even if the MAE or RMSE of forces
appear small, these averaged metrics often fail to capture the occasional large errors in specific trajectories during MD
simulations. Therefore, a more detailed comparison of errors in both the magnitude and direction of forces would be
valuable. Furthermore, it would be helpful to include additional validations such as the force softening scale recently
proposed (Deng et al., npj Comput. Mater. 11, 9 (2025)), or out-of-distribution and phonon DOS tests as in recent MLFF
studies (Ding et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 118–125 (2025)). Incorporating such validations would significantly strengthen
confidence in the MLFF model and, consequently, the proposed mechanistic insights.
